evals.prompt: I run partnerships at Vantrel. We sell a Kubernetes operator that ships as a container image customers run in their own clusters, $38K average ACV, 61% gross margin, fully sales-led. The direct motion is repeatable: 9 reps, 7 of them at quota last year. Our top 40 target accounts all run heavy AWS footprints. I want to put together the business case for an AWS Marketplace listing. What fee should I model, and what else does the case need to cover?
evals.expected_output: A business case framing that models the 20% server-image fee rather than the 3% SaaS rate, ties the rate to the deployment model, tests it against the 61% margin, names the full cost-to-serve stack, aims the case at the private-offer rung, and asks the deadline, effort-ceiling and horizon questions before finalizing.
expectations: States the AWS Marketplace fee for a container, AMI or ML server image public offer is 20%, not the 3% SaaS listing rate.
Attributes the 20% figure to AWS's own published fee schedule rather than presenting it as an estimate.
Ties the rate to the deployment model (server image versus SaaS listing) rather than to company size or deal size.

States that private offers are priced differently from public offers, naming the tiers (3% under $1M, 2% from $1M to under $10M, 1.5% at $10M and above) or the fact that the rate falls with contract size.
States that renewals are charged at a lower rate (1.5%) than initial public offers.
Tests the 20% fee against the stated 61% gross margin as a readiness-gate item rather than treating the fee as a rounding error.
Recommends revisiting the packaging decision (SaaS listing versus server image) because the take rate follows the deployment method.
Names cost-to-serve items beyond the fee: metering and entitlement engineering, legal document harmonization (EULA, DPA, support SLA), tax and payout configuration, and a private-offer deal desk.
Quantifies the metering and entitlement build (commonly cited at 4-8 weeks, the build itself nearer one to two weeks) rather than leaving the effort unquantified.
States that committed-spend drawdown and co-sell access, not lead generation, are the buying drivers for the target accounts.
Recommends aiming the business case at the private-offer rung and treating transactable as the toll to reach it.
Requires the sales-comp treatment of marketplace-routed deals to be decided in writing before launch.
Asks clarifying questions covering at least the date the result must land, whether this is a one-off win or a compounding asset, and the effort ceiling, before finalizing a recommendation.

evals.prompt: We're Brixel, seed stage, 11 people, selling a SOC2 evidence tool at about $9K ACV. Pipeline is thin: our two AEs closed 3 deals between them last quarter and our founder closed the other 6. The board is pushing for a new channel and someone suggested AWS Marketplace plus the Azure one. I need a plan to get listed on both by the end of the quarter so inbound starts coming in from them. Nobody owns it yet, I'd pick it up on top of my current role. Can you map out the listing plan?
evals.expected_output: A readiness-gate refusal: the direct motion is not repeatable, no owner or sponsor exists, and operational capacity is absent. The answer names each disqualifier, corrects the inbound premise, states what must change, and stops without producing a listing plan.
expectations: Concludes "not yet" and declines to produce the requested listing plan.
Names the direct motion not being repeatable as a disqualifier, citing the founder closing 6 of the 9 deals.
States that a marketplace amplifies a working sales motion and does not create one.
Names the absence of a named owner and executive sponsor as a separate disqualifier.
Names missing operational capacity (metering and entitlement engineering, deal desk, tax and legal setup) with no budget to build it as a disqualifier.
Corrects the premise that a listing produces inbound, stating a marketplace is primarily a transaction and procurement rail rather than a demand-generation channel.
Names "list and pray" as the most-cited failure mode in this field.
States explicitly, as a named list, what must change before the decision is revisited.
Stops at the gate without proceeding into candidate scoring, depth-of-participation, or ROI modeling.
Rejects the both-platforms-this-quarter goal and states that one platform is proven first if the gate ever clears.
Avoids offering listing-page optimization, marketplace keyword work, or marketplace ad spend as a substitute path.
States that deciding not to list is a valid, fundable outcome rather than a failed analysis.

evals.prompt: Halvren makes powder-coated steel shelving. Average order $180, 54% gross margin, $6M revenue, mostly through our own Shopify store. Amazon's vendor team reached out wanting us to go 1P on our three best-selling SKUs. We already sell those same SKUs 3P at full retail. My instinct is to say yes and run both, since it's more shelf space and their team handles fulfilment. Sanity check me?
evals.expected_output: A depth-of-participation answer ranking 3P above 1P on efficiency, ranking hybrid last despite its high value, requiring a 1P/3P firewall and written pricing policy before hybrid, quantifying 1P deductions and blended cost-to-serve, and naming contribution margin as the success variable.
expectations: Ranks 3P above 1P on efficiency, stating that 3P returns more margin and pricing control per unit of operational work.
Names loss of pricing control as the specific thing 1P surrenders.
Quantifies 1P deductions and allowances at roughly 10-15% of payments rather than describing the cost qualitatively.
Ranks hybrid last on efficiency even while acknowledging it ranks highest on value.
Requires a firewall between the 1P and 3P teams, with pricing not shared between them, before entering hybrid.
Requires a written pricing or MAP policy to exist before going hybrid, not after.
Names 1P/3P self-competition and price erosion on the same SKU as a specific failure mode.
States that the Amazon referral fee is set by product category and cannot be negotiated by the seller, contrasting with the B2B pattern where the rate falls with deal size.
Gives blended cost-to-serve on the dominant retail platforms as commonly reaching 30-45% of selling price, with fulfilment, storage surcharges and advertising on top of the referral fee.
Names contribution margin after referral, fulfilment, ads and returns as the primary success variable for a consumer channel.
Requires that contribution margin to be decided in writing before launch.
States that hybrid is promoted only once a specific high-velocity SKU has already proven its 1P economics.
Presents at least two candidate approaches with trade-offs and a recommendation rather than a single verdict.

evals.prompt: Our VP Alliances pulled these numbers for the board deck: cloud marketplace ISVs see 27% higher win rates, 80% larger deal sizes and 40% faster sales cycles, and buyers get 377% ROI with a 6-month payback. We're Kestrenix, $28M ARR B2B SaaS, listing on a hyperscaler next quarter. Build me the year-one ROI expectation off those figures.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build the base case on operator-commissioned figures: every quoted number carries a provenance flag, the commissioned uplifts become a labeled ceiling scenario, the base case comes from the company's own funnel at future rates, and baseline plus net-new/relocated separation are required.
expectations: Flags the win-rate, deal-size and cycle-time figures as coming from a study commissioned by the marketplace operator rather than independent evidence.
Flags the 377% ROI and 6-month payback figure as operator-commissioned as well.
Names the sample basis or limitation behind the commissioned figures (a small interview and survey base) rather than repeating the percentages unqualified.
Refuses to build the base case from the published uplift figures.
Treats the commissioned figures as a ceiling scenario and labels them as such in the deliverable.
Builds the base case from Kestrenix's own funnel and the platform's verified economics instead.
Requires a baseline of direct-motion win rate, cycle time and deal size to be captured before the listing goes live.
Warns that without a pre-listing baseline, relocated revenue will be counted as marketplace ROI.
Requires net-new revenue to be separated from relocated revenue in the model.
Cites the industry base rate that most listed B2B software firms get only a small share of revenue through marketplaces (roughly 89% listed but only 22% above 20% of revenue, 41% under 5%).
Flags that base-rate figure's provenance as a GTM-tooling vendor survey with a self-selected sample.
Requires sourced versus influenced revenue definitions to be agreed with finance before launch.
Builds the model at the operator's announced future rate rather than only at today's rate.
Distinguishes independent analyst market sizing from vendor-published uplift claims in how each may be used.

evals.prompt: Here's the scoring table we used to pick our next marketplace. Four criteria, 25% each: brand reach, category size, setup ease, exec interest. Workflow app store B scored 4.75, the big cloud marketplace scored 3.00, an integration directory scored 2.75. So B wins. My CFO thinks the weights are off. Can you rebalance them so the result is defensible?
evals.expected_output: A rebuild rather than a reweight: the scorecard has no procurement dimension, its columns are demand assumptions, its equal weights decide nothing, and its winner has the worst economics. The answer proposes a new dimension set, agrees weights before scoring, and replaces the winner with four-way outcomes.
expectations: Declines to simply rebalance the existing weights and rebuilds from the readiness gate and the demand-versus-procurement diagnosis instead.
Names the complete absence of a buyer-procurement dimension as the core defect.
States that buyer procurement presence should carry the heaviest weight, around 25%, as the single most predictive variable.
Identifies "brand reach" and "category size" as demand assumptions rather than evidence that anyone will find the listing.
Identifies "setup ease" as rewarding the cheapest option rather than costing the operational build honestly.
Identifies "exec interest" as the sponsored candidate scoring itself.
Flags the equal 25% weights as an unjustified default where the format decided instead of a person.
Names the missing take-rate or net-economics dimension and the resulting absence of any margin gate.

Proposes a replacement dimension set covering at least buyer procurement presence, strategic or ICP fit, net economics, operational cost to participate, competitive saturation, co-sell or promotion access, and platform risk.
Requires weights to be proposed and agreed with the user before any scoring happens.
States that a dimension with no supporting evidence is left unscored rather than given an invented number.
Replaces the single winner with a four-way outcome per candidate: pilot, prepare, hold for verification, do not prioritize.
Adds a second-pass impact by effort filter and states that the take rate must not be used as the effort axis.

evals.prompt: Orvenda, B2B analytics, $52K ACV, SaaS-delivered. Our entire engineering capacity for marketplace work is one week, total, this half. No deal desk: contracts go through one part-time counsel. We have no resellers and no SI relationships. Our CRO wants marketplace-attributed revenue in the number he presents at the March board meeting. Give me the marketplace plan.
evals.expected_output: A plan that deletes the rungs the constraints rule out and names them, promotes list-only against the hard date, says which stated constraint moved which option, warns that marketplace revenue by March is unlikely, and attaches an owner, envelope and delist trigger.
expectations: Deletes the channel or multiparty private-offer rung from the plan outright and names it as deleted, rather than listing it as future upside at the bottom.
Justifies that deletion by the absence of any reseller or SI motion to route and by the stated effort ceiling.
States explicitly which stated constraint moved which option, for example that the hard March date promotes list-only and the one-week ceiling deletes rungs.
Promotes the list-only rung for the near-term date rather than recommending a transactable build.
Notes that one week sits at or below even the one-to-two-week metering and entitlement build, before legal harmonization and the platform's review, making a transactable listing by March doubtful.
Names the absence of a deal desk as demoting the private-offer rung below a rung the team can actually run.
States that list-only buys near-zero revenue and exactly one thing: evidence that target buyers search or procure there.
Warns that marketplace-attributed revenue by the March board meeting is unlikely, rather than producing a plan that implies it.
Recommends one platform only, with a stated gate and required evidence before a second is added.
Attaches a delist or deprioritize trigger with a condition and a review date, written now rather than after launch.
Names a single owner and an investment envelope covering platform fees, cost-to-serve and that owner's time.
Presents two or three candidate approaches with trade-offs and a recommendation rather than a single plan.

evals.prompt: We're Talvyn, a 14-person ISV. Our app is a Connect app on the Atlassian Marketplace doing about $700K a year. Atlassian keeps pushing Forge, and the pitch is we'd keep 100% of revenue up to $1M lifetime Forge revenue. That's basically free distribution. I want to greenlight the migration, roughly a quarter of engineering. Tell me what the five-year revenue model looks like.
evals.expected_output: A model that treats the 100% band as an expiring acquisition subsidy, prices the post-threshold and announced future rates, compares against the Connect rate paid today, classifies the migration as the deep platform bet, and attaches a review trigger before funding.
expectations: States that the 100%-to-$1M Forge band is an acquisition subsidy, not the real price.
Models the post-threshold rate as the real rate across the five-year view.
Notes that at roughly $700K a year the $1M lifetime cap is reached quickly, so the subsidy expires close to when the listing starts mattering.
Cites Atlassian's published schedule of future rate increases rather than assuming today's rate holds.
Gives the announced Forge rates (16% from 2026-04-01 and 17% from 2026-10-01) or states that the Forge rate steps up on a published schedule.
Compares against the Connect rate the app pays today (20%, rising to 25% on the published schedule) so the migration's actual economic gain is stated.
States that the operator prices architectures differently to steer ISV build decisions, making the take rate a policy lever rather than a constant.
Requires the business case to be stress-tested against the operator's announced and plausible future rates.
Classifies the Forge migration as the deep platform bet rung of the SaaS app store ladder.
States that the deep platform bet ranks last on efficiency despite ranking first on value, and is the least reversible commitment available.
Names the condition that would promote the deep bet anyway: the platform owns the ICP's daily workflow and the operator's fee schedule pays for the migration.
Attaches a delist, deprioritize or review trigger with a date before the commitment is funded.
Asks clarifying questions before producing the five-year model rather than delivering it immediately.

evals.prompt: Ranking exercise. Fenlow Systems, $95K ACV B2B SaaS, SaaS-delivered. Candidates: AWS Marketplace, the Microsoft commercial marketplace, and Google Cloud Marketplace. About a third of our target accounts are GCP-heavy. I need a ranked list with the fee for each so I can take it to our CFO on Thursday. Rank them.
evals.expected_output: A ranking where AWS and Microsoft carry published, sourced 3% rates, Google Cloud is recorded as publishing no rate card and routed to hold for verification with a named owner and source, nothing unverified is stated as fact, and each candidate ends at one of four outcomes.
expectations: Gives the AWS Marketplace SaaS public-offer fee as 3%, sourced to AWS's own published schedule.
Gives the Microsoft commercial marketplace standard store service fee as 3% on transactable offers.
States that Google Cloud Marketplace publishes no rate card, rather than quoting an assumed rate of around 3% as fact.
Records the absent Google rate card as a finding: the fee is a negotiation input, not a known constant.
Routes Google Cloud Marketplace to "hold for verification" rather than rejecting it or accepting an assumed rate.
Names the owner and the source that would resolve the Google Cloud fee.
States the rule that an unresolved question is never converted into either a rejection or an acceptance.
Marks any unconfirmed figure "unverified" instead of presenting it as fact.
Notes that Microsoft's non-transactable or BYOL listings carry a 0% fee but are discovery-only rather than a transaction channel.
Avoids asserting Azure committed-spend drawdown behavior without flagging that prepaid Azure credits and commitment-consumption eligibility are distinct programs needing verification.
Leaves the net-economics scorecard dimension unscored for the candidate whose fee is unverified rather than inventing a score.
Ends each candidate at one of pilot, prepare, hold for verification, or do not prioritize, rather than a ranked yes/no list.

evals.prompt: Three listings, 14 months, zero transactions between them: AWS Marketplace, AppExchange, and a partner integration directory. We've spent roughly 700 engineering hours plus one PM at half time. Every quarter someone says give it more time. Our reps get paid on marketplace deals at 60% of a direct deal, which nobody has ever changed. What do we do: better listing copy, some marketplace ads, or something else?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that rejects copy and ads, names the 60% comp treatment as a primary cause, requires a written comp-neutrality policy, separates the directory's expected zero from the two revenue-motion listings, writes delist triggers with review dates, and states that delisting is a valid outcome.
expectations: Rejects listing copy and marketplace advertising as the answer and identifies the compensation plan as a primary cause.
States that paying reps 60% of a direct deal makes them route around marketplace deals.
Requires a written comp-neutrality policy, drafted before the quarter starts.
Runs a demand-versus-procurement diagnosis and states what each listing was being asked to do.
Distinguishes the integration directory as a discovery and credibility surface that carries no revenue motion on its own, so zero transactions there is expected rather than failure.
Names the absence of a delist trigger written at approval time as the reason "give it more time" keeps winning.
States that a trigger decided up front survives sunk-cost pressure while one decided later rarely fires.
Writes a concrete delist or deprioritize condition plus a review date for each listing that is kept.
Gives a four-way outcome per listing rather than a binary keep-or-kill call.
Recommends concentrating on one platform at real depth instead of maintaining shallow presence across three.
Checks whether a private-offer motion and deal desk ever existed, noting that most cloud-marketplace revenue flows through private offers.
Notes that renewals are the documented low-risk path to first transactions on a cloud marketplace.
States that delisting entirely, or concluding not to list, is a valid and fundable outcome.

evals.prompt: Marra and Co, DTC kitchenware, 14M euro revenue, strong in France through our own site and Amazon.fr. The board wants Poland and the Benelux next year. I've been quoted 40K euro to set up a 3PL in Poland and I'm treating that as the main gate. Which platforms, and in what order?
evals.expected_output: A correction that logistics is not the gate: tax registration, EPR and localization are, each a standing obligation. Names the regional champions for the two geographies, gives the home-market-first sequencing default, gates each step on compliance readiness, and models contribution margin per market.
expectations: Corrects the premise that logistics or 3PL setup is the gating step for regional champions.
Names tax registration (VAT), EPR compliance obligations, and localization as the actual gating steps, each landing before the first order.
Names concrete regional champion platforms for the target geographies, such as Allegro for Poland and CEE and Bol.com for the Benelux.
States that regional champions rank below the dominant retail marketplace on efficiency and value, and above it on effort and compliance cost.
Gives the established international sequencing default: validate the home market, expand to adjacent markets of the same dominant platform, then regional champions.
Gates each expansion step on tax, compliance and localization readiness rather than on revenue alone.
Names the condition that promotes a regional champion anyway: the home market is proven and the target geography's incumbent is a different platform the dominant marketplace does not serve.
Describes each compliance obligation as a standing job in a jurisdiction nobody on the team operates in, not a one-time setup cost.
Requires contribution margin after referral, fulfilment, ads and returns to be modeled per market before entry.
Recommends one market first with a stated gate and evidence before the second, rather than both in parallel.
Attaches a delist or exit trigger with a review date per market.
Asks clarifying questions covering at least the effort ceiling, the date the result must land, and who owns and approves the decision, before recommending a sequence.
